# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's case for time travel

## 1. The question, frozen

The document answers several things (why the model vanishes, why the Time Traveller looks battered on his return), but its opening makes one thing central: the Time Traveller spends all of Chapter I building a case that travelling in time is *achievable in principle*, against a room that assumes it is nonsense. That is the explanation under test here, over the range of Chapter I and II (before any journey is reported). Kind of question: closest to "why can something not happen?", run backwards — an apparent block (you cannot move in time) is being argued away rather than defended.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1 — No instantaneous solid.** Nothing without duration is real, so any real thing has four extents: Length, Breadth, Thickness, Duration.
- **P2 — Time differs from space only in one respect.** Consciousness moves along Time, involuntarily, at a uniform rate from birth to death; that is the *only* difference from the other three dimensions.
- **P3 — Blocks can be engineered around.** Gravity once made vertical motion nearly impossible; balloons removed that block without adding a dimension. By the same logic, a machine might remove the apparent block on moving along Time.
- **P4 — The demonstration.** A lever is pressed; the model vanishes from the table.
- **P5 — The patch for an awkward case.** When it's objected that a past-bound machine should have been visible on every earlier night in that room, the Psychologist supplies "presentation below the threshold, diluted presentation" — a fast enough object registers faintly, like a spinning spoke.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 (no instantaneous solid) | **Idle** | Remove it and go straight to "time is a fourth dimension": P2 and P3 do exactly the same work. It dresses up the definition but holds nothing that P2/P3 don't already hold. |
| P2 (consciousness moves at uniform, involuntary rate) | **Loose** | Swap "consciousness" for any other one-way, involuntary carrier ("an unseen current sweeps things forward") and both jobs it serves — explaining ordinary one-directionality, licensing the idea of resisting it — survive unchanged. What's actually held is only *there is some default, non-optional, one-way drift*; naming it "consciousness" is decoration. |
| P3 (balloon analogy) | **Borrowed** | It rests on gravity's restriction and time's restriction being the *same kind* of restriction. That equivalence is never tested — it's imported, not shown. Doing real rhetorical work (making "permanent block" feel like "temporary limit"), but not real evidentiary work. |
| P4 (the vanishing) | **Held if** | Held, if no trick was used — but "no trick" is exactly what the Medical Man and the narrator flag as unsettled ("are you in earnest... or is this a trick — like that ghost you showed us"). The text answers this with confidence, not with a check. So this part is held only by a doubtful job: ruling out sleight-of-hand. |
| P5 (diluted presentation) | **Loose / catch-all, no gauge** | Volunteered instantly, by a bystander rather than the theory's owner, the moment the sharpest objection (why wasn't it visible on past nights) lands, and accepted with visible relief ("helps the paradox delightfully"). No one says how much dilution a given speed should produce, so there's no way to tell this from a story that would explain *any* failure to see the machine. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** Had the model instead sat still, or reappeared a second later, could the same four-dimension theory have absorbed that too ("it went only a very short way")? Nothing on offer says what result *would* have counted against the theory — every outcome looks confirmable.
- **Reverse / where it came from.** The Time Traveller says he "had a vague inkling of a machine" before working out the geometry, and admits after the demonstration that he doesn't know whether it went forward or backward. A theory built to license a machine he already wanted, and happy either way the model went, is asserted rather than built: it doesn't commit to a direction it could be caught out on.
- **Pull.** P1/P2 pull against each other. P1 wants time to be symmetric with space; P2 (the only-difference-is-consciousness clause) is exactly what makes it *not* symmetric in practice. The text raises this itself (the Medical Man's "why cannot we move about in Time"), and P2 is the answer — but that answer quietly does less work for symmetry than P1 claimed.
- **What the change list leaves out.** No poke is offered that "should matter" alongside one that "should not" (Step 5's pairing). Everything supplied is a confirmation; nothing is staged as a possible disconfirmation.
- **Where the parts came from.** Asserted, throughout — stated in dialogue, accepted by an audience that is explicitly credulous ("Of course," "that's plain enough"), not fitted against prior cases or built to survive a case not yet met.

## 5. What would tighten it most

One added job would do more than anything else here: have the Time Traveller state, before pressing the lever, one specific thing that should *not* happen if the theory is right (a fully worked prediction, not "it will vanish"). Second, give P5 a measurable form — a speed-to-faintness relation — so it could be checked rather than simply invoked. Third, settle the forward/backward question independently of the demonstration; a theory equally content with either result is explaining less than it appears to.

## 6. What this does not show

None of this touches whether time travel is physically possible, only whether the *stated reasons* for believing so hold each other up within Chapter I and II. A true claim can rest on loose parts (P2, P5 here), and this test does not weigh against Wells's aim, which is to make a story feel plausible for an evening, not to survive a physics seminar.

## 7. One next step

Press the one gap the text itself opens and then drops: Filby demands "experimental verification" and the Time Traveller promises it, but the only verification supplied is the very demonstration under question. The next useful move is to ask what a check *independent* of watching the model vanish would look like — e.g., some trace the model should leave behind if it truly persisted through the interval, as opposed to simply being hidden by a mechanism.
